newsitem.title: USA: Jurors hear tape of Oklahoma City explosion.
newsitem.headline: Jurors hear tape of Oklahoma City explosion.

text.p: The massive roar of an explosion filled the courtroom in the Oklahoma City bombing trial Friday as jurors listened to a dramatic tape recording of the blast.

The tape, the first evidence introduced in the federal murder and conspiracy case against Timothy McVeigh, recorded a 9 a.m. hearing of the Oklahoma Water Resources Board on April 19, 1995, across the street from the Alfred P. Murrah federal building.
After about two minutes of voices, the tape is interrupted by a huge roar, crashes, rumblings and the frightened shout of "Let's get out of here."
The 9:02 a.m. blast at the Murrah building killed 168 people, including several young children in a day-care centre.
"The building shook and the whole ceiling fell down," the water board's attorney, Lou Klaver, told the courtroom. She was the first witness to testify in the emotionally charged trial.
"I didn't know how we were going to get out ... We were all disoriented," she recalled. Outside, she said "it looked like a war zone."
The prosecution claims McVeigh, motivated by anti-government hatred and extremist politics, blew up the federal building in hopes of provoking a "second American Revolution."

Defence attorney Stephen Jones has tried to undermine the government's case against his client by raising questions about the possibility of an uncaptured accomplice, confused eyewitnesses and the FBI's handling of the evidence.

McVeigh, 29, wearing an open-necked white shirt and khaki trousers, kept his head down during the morning's testimony and took notes. The tall, thin Gulf War veteran has pleaded not guilty and could face the death penalty if convicted.

He was expressionless as the second witness, former Marine Corps recruiter Michael Norfleet, testified that the bomb "filleted open" his right eye, leaving him partly blind and destroying his dreams of being a pilot.

Norfleet recalled parking that morning in front of a Ryder truck outside the federal building. The truck was used to hold the powerful bomb, and Norfleet said he had thought it was odd at the time that the truck was there.
The third prosecution witness, television cameraman Phila Monahan, also described the scene for jurors. He said a pillar of smoke from the blast could be seen from 10 miles (16 km) away.
The attorney for the water board testified that a clock fell off the wall when the blast hit. The clock's hands stopped at 9:02, she said.
